derivations.claim:
By [F1], write $B=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$. Thus $R$ exists, is normal, and
$$x^{\mathsf T}Rx=\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{\lambda_j-z},\qquad
\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)=\eta\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{(\lambda_j-u)^2+\eta^2}.$$
If $x\ne0$, this imaginary part is strictly positive, so $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$; if $x=0$, the denominator is $1$.

Direct multiplication verifies
$$(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)\left(R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx}\right)=I.$$
Since $B+xx^{\mathsf T}$ is also real symmetric and $z\notin\mathbb R$, its resolvent exists; hence the displayed expression is $R_x$.

Taking traces in step 2.1 gives
$$\operatorname{tr}(R_x-R)=-\frac{x^{\mathsf T}R^2x}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx}.$$
In the eigenbasis of [F1],
$$|x^{\mathsf T}R^2x|\le\sum_j\frac{(U^{\mathsf T}x)_j^2}{(\lambda_j-u)^2+\eta^2}
=\frac{\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)}{\eta}.$$
Also $|1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx|\ge\operatorname{Im}(x^{\mathsf T}Rx)$ when $x\ne0$; for $x=0$ the trace difference is zero. Combining these inequalities proves the stated $1/\eta$ bound.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $B$ be a real symmetric non-negative $d\times d$ matrix, let $x\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Put $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^{\mathsf T}-zI)^{-1}$. Then $1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx\ne0$,
$$R_x=R-\frac{Rxx^{\mathsf T}R}{1+x^{\mathsf T}Rx},$$
and
$$\left|\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R\right|\le\frac1\eta.$$

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

derivations.claim: Fix all vectors except $Y_{n,j}$. Replacing that vector by another vector $Y'_{n,j}$ changes $B_n$ by removing $Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$ and adding $Y'_{n,j}(Y'_{n,j})^{\mathsf T}$. Applying [F1] once to remove the first term and once to add the second shows that $\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}$ changes by at most $2/\eta$. Hence each of the real and imaginary parts of $M_n(z)$ has coordinate oscillation at most $c_j=2/(d_n\eta)$.

Apply [F2] separately to $\operatorname{Re}M_n(z)$ and $\operatorname{Im}M_n(z)$. If a complex number has modulus greater than $t$, at least one of its real or imaginary parts has magnitude greater than $t/\sqrt2$. The union bound therefore gives
$$\Pr\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\}
\le4\exp\left(-\frac{t^2d_n^2\eta^2}{4n}\right).$$
This is the stated estimate.
Since $d_n/n\to c>0$, for each fixed $t>0$ the exponent in step 2.1 is at most $-c_tn$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for some $c_t>0$. The probabilities are therefore summable.
Apply [F3] to the events in step 3.1 for each $t=1/k$, $k\ge1$, and intersect the resulting countable collection of probability-one events. On that event $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$.

For $\gamma>0$, set
$$a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad r_+:=\max\{r,0\}\quad(r\in\mathbb R).$$
Define the Marchenko–Pastur set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ by
$$\mu_\gamma(A):=\int_{A\cap(a_\gamma,b_\gamma)}\frac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x}\,d\lambda(x)+\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0(A),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. The formula defines a finite Borel measure; its total mass is established by the Marchenko–Pastur law below.

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
Put $B=2\sqrt\gamma$, $A_0=1+\gamma$, and $x(\theta)=A_0+B\cos\theta$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. This substitution maps $(0,\pi)$ onto $(a,b)$ in reverse order, with $\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}=B\sin\theta$ and $|dx|=B\sin\theta\,d\theta$. Thus the continuous part of $\mu_\gamma$ becomes $(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta/x(\theta)$. For real $A>B$, the substitution $t=\tan(\theta/2)$ gives
$$\int_0^\pi\frac{d\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}=2\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{(A+B)+(A-B)t^2}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{A^2-B^2}}.$$
Write $I_0(A)=\int_0^\pi(A+B\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{A^2-B^2}$. Since $\int_0^\pi\cos\theta\,d\theta=0$ and $\cos\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)=B^{-1}-A/[B(A+B\cos\theta)]$,
$$I_1(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=\frac\pi B-\frac A B I_0(A),\quad I_2(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=-\frac A B I_1(A)=-\frac{A\pi}{B^2}+\frac{A^2}{B^2}I_0(A).$$
Therefore
$$J(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}\,d\theta=I_0(A)-I_2(A)=\frac{\pi(A-\sqrt{A^2-B^2})}{B^2}.$$
For $A=A_0>B$, the root is $|1-\gamma|$; if $\gamma=1$, direct cancellation $\sin^2\theta/(2+2\cos\theta)= (1-\cos\theta)/2$ gives the same value by continuity. Hence the continuous mass is $2J(A_0)/\pi=(A_0-|1-\gamma|)/(2\gamma)=\min(1,\gamma)/\gamma$. Adding $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ gives total mass one; the density is nonnegative and integrable by this finite integral, and its support is nonnegative.

For $w=re^{i\theta}\in\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$, with $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta<\pi$, define $q_0(w)=\sqrt r\,e^{i\theta/2}$. This is continuous, satisfies $q_0(w)^2=w$, and is holomorphic: for $h\to0$ with $w+h$ in the slit plane,
$$\frac{q_0(w+h)-q_0(w)}h=\frac1{q_0(w+h)+q_0(w)}\longrightarrow\frac1{2q_0(w)}.$$
Set $\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,B]$ and $q(A)=q_0(A-B)q_0(A+B)$ for $A\in\Omega$. Both factors are defined and holomorphic there, $q(A)^2=A^2-B^2$, and $q(A)>0$ for real $A>B$. The domain is connected: each $A-B=re^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$ can be joined inside it to $B+1$ by continuously changing $r$ to $1$ and $\theta$ to $0$. The integral $J(A)$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$. Indeed, on any compact subset its denominator is bounded away from zero, and the difference quotient of its integrand tends pointwise to $-\sin^2\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)^2$ with a uniform integrable bound; [F3] justifies passing that limit through the integral. The identity theorem [F2] extends the formula from real $A>B$ (which has limit points inside $\Omega$) to all $A\in\Omega$. In particular it applies to $A_z=A_0-z$, whose imaginary part is negative.

Let $q=\sqrt{(1+\gamma-z)^2-4\gamma}$ on that branch. The substitution in step 1.1 and $1/[x(x-z)]=z^{-1}((x-z)^{-1}-x^{-1})$ give the transform of the continuous part as $[(A_z-q)-(A_0-|1-\gamma|)]/(2\gamma z)$. Adding the atom contributes $-(1-1/\gamma)_+/z$; simplifying in the cases $\gamma\le1$ and $\gamma>1$ gives
$$m_\gamma(z)=\frac{1-\gamma-z-q}{2\gamma z}.$$
Since $q^2=(1-\gamma-z)^2-4\gamma z$, substitution verifies $\gamma z m_\gamma(z)^2+(z+\gamma-1)m_\gamma(z)+1=0$, which is the fixed-point equation in the Statement.

For $x\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}(z/(x-z))=\eta x/|x-z|^2\ge0$. Integrating this identity against the probability measure from step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{Im}(z m_\gamma(z))\ge0$, so $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z))=-\eta-\gamma\operatorname{Im}(z m_\gamma(z))\le-\eta$.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, its Stieltjes transform, with the $(x-z)^{-1}$ convention, is
$$m_\mu(z):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\mu(x).$$
The integral is finite because $|x-z|^{-1}\le\eta^{-1}$ for every real $x$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim:
For $\eta>0$, the imaginary part of the integrand in [F1] is $\eta/((x-u)^2+\eta^2)$. Fubini [F2] therefore gives
$$\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du=\int K_{\eta,a,b}(x)\,d\mu(x),\quad K_{\eta,a,b}(x)=\frac1\pi\left(\arctan\frac{b-x}{\eta}-\arctan\frac{a-x}{\eta}\right).$$
The kernel lies in $[0,1]$ and tends pointwise to $1$ on $(a,b)$, $1/2$ at either endpoint, and $0$ elsewhere. [F3] gives the interval formula in the Statement, including endpoint atoms.

For any $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\eta\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta)=\int\frac{\eta^2}{(t-x)^2+\eta^2}\,d\mu(t).$$
The integrand is bounded by $1$ and tends to $\mathbf1_{\{x\}}(t)$ as $\eta\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence [F3] proves the atom formula.
If $m_\mu=m_\nu$, step 1.2 gives equality of their point masses at every $x$. Step 1.1 then gives $\mu((a,b))=\nu((a,b))$ for every $a<b$.

The family $\mathcal P=\{\varnothing,\mathbb R\}\cup\{(a,b):a<b\}$ is a pi-system: the intersection of two open intervals is another open interval or empty. It generates the Borel sigma-algebra because open intervals form a basis. The class of Borel sets on which $\mu$ and $\nu$ agree is a lambda-system: it contains $\mathbb R$ because both measures are probabilities, is closed under complements by finite total mass, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by countable additivity. Step 2.1 and [F4] therefore give equality on every Borel set, so $\mu=\nu$.

be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], diagonalize $T=U\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_d)U^*$ with each $t_j\ge0$. Then $T^{1/2}:=U\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{t_1},\ldots,\sqrt{t_d})U^*$ is Hermitian positive semidefinite. With $B=N^{-1/2}T^{1/2}X$, the matrix $A=BB^*$ is Hermitian and $v^*Av=\|B^*v\|_2^2\ge0$ for every $v$; hence all its eigenvalues are nonnegative.

Each displayed set function is a finite nonnegative linear combination of the point masses defined in [F2], which are Borel probability measures by [F3]; its coefficients are nonnegative because $\operatorname{rank}(P_\lambda)/d\ge0$ and $\|P_\lambda x\|_2^2\ge0$. Thus both are finite Borel measures. By step 1.1 their finite supports lie in $[0,\infty)$.

$$q:=x^*Rx=\sum_j\frac{|c_j|^2}{\lambda_j-z},\qquad \operatorname{Im}q=\eta\sum_j\frac{|c_j|^2}{|\lambda_j-z|^2}=\eta\|Rx\|_2^2.$$

$$ (B+xx^*-zI)\left(R-\frac{Rxx^*R}{1+x^*Rx}\right)=I.$$

The case $x=0$ has both differences zero.

Let $\xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d)^\mathsf T$ have independent identically distributed complex coordinates with $\mathbb E\xi_i=0$, $\mathbb E|\xi_i|^2=1$, and $\mu_4:=\mathbb E|\xi_i|^4<\infty$. Let $A$ be an independent random complex $d\times d$ matrix with $\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2<\infty$, where $\|A\|_F^2:=\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2$. Put $\tau:=\mathbb E\xi_1^2$. Then
$$\mathbb E\left|\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2\le C_{\mu_4,\tau}\,\mathbb E\|A\|_F^2,\qquad C_{\mu_4,\tau}:=\max\{\mu_4-1,1+|\tau|^2\}.$$

Let $B\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite, let $x\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Set $R=(B-zI)^{-1}$ and $R_x=(B+xx^*-zI)^{-1}$. For the trace norm $\|M\|_1$, defined as the sum of the singular values of $M$, one has $1+x^*Rx\ne0$,
$$R_x=R-\frac{Rxx^*R}{1+x^*Rx},\qquad \|R_x-R\|_1\le\frac1\eta,\qquad |\operatorname{tr}R_x-\operatorname{tr}R|\le\frac1\eta.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, unit second absolute moment, and absolute value at most $K$, where $K$ is independent of $n$. Let $T_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite with $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M$, and let $x_n\in\mathbb C^n$ be deterministic with $\|x_n\|_2=1$. Assume $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. For fixed $z=u+i\eta$ with $\eta>0$, set
$$A_n:=\frac1{N_n}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2},\qquad R_n(z):=(A_n-zI)^{-1}.$$
Then $x_n^*R_n(z)x_n-\mathbb E[x_n^*R_n(z)x_n]\to0$ almost surely. Moreover, for every $t>0$ there is a constant $C=C(K,M,z,\kappa)$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left\{|x_n^*R_n(z)x_n-\mathbb E[x_n^*R_n(z)x_n]|>t\right\}\le\frac{C}{t^4N_n^2}.$$

derivations.claim:
Fix $n,z$, suppress the index $n$, write $N=N_n$, $s_j=T^{1/2}X_{\cdot j}/\sqrt N$, $R=(A-zI)^{-1}$, $R_j=(A-s_js_j^*-zI)^{-1}$, and $\beta_j=(1+s_j^*R_js_j)^{-1}$. The companion matrix $\widetilde A=N^{-1}X^*TX$ is positive semidefinite by [F4], so $q=N^{-1}\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde A-zI)^{-1}$ is the Stieltjes transform of an expected probability measure on $[0,\infty)$ by [F5] and has positive imaginary part. If $q=\int(\lambda-z)^{-1}\,dG(\lambda)$, then for every $t\ge0$,
$$\operatorname{Im}\{z(1+tq)\}=\eta+t\int\frac{\lambda\eta}{|\lambda-z|^2}\,dG(\lambda)\ge\eta,$$
so $C:=(I+qT)^{-1}$ exists and $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le |z|/\eta$. The same spectral calculation applied to $A-s_js_j^*$ gives $|\beta_j|\le |z|/\eta$.

Set $b_j=(1+N^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(TR_j))^{-1}$ and $\xi_j=s_j^*R_js_j-N^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(TR_j)$. The trace in $b_j$ is a Stieltjes transform with nonnegative weights: in an eigenbasis of $A-s_js_j^*$ its weights are $\langle v_k,Tv_k\rangle/N\ge0$. The inequality in step 1.1 therefore also gives $|b_j|\le |z|/\eta$. Conditional on all columns except $j$, [F1] and $\|T^{1/2}R_jT^{1/2}\|_F^2\le nM^2/\eta^2$ give $\mathbb E_j|\xi_j|^2\le C_1 n/N^2=O(N^{-1})$, where $\mathbb E_j$ integrates column $j$. For any deterministic unit $x$, set
$$\alpha_j=x^*Cs_js_j^*R_jx-N^{-1}x^*CTR_jx.$$
This is a centered quadratic form in column $j$. Its coefficient matrix has rank at most one and Frobenius norm at most $M\|C\|/\eta$, so [F1] gives $\mathbb E_j|\alpha_j|^2=O(N^{-2})$. Also $\mathbb E_j\alpha_j=0$ and $\beta_j-b_j=-\beta_jb_j\xi_j$.

For all sufficiently large $n$ we have $N=N_n\ge2$. Put $Y=[s_2\ \cdots\ s_N]$, $D=Y^*Y-zI_{N-1}$, and $C_-=YY^*-zI_n=A-s_1s_1^*-zI_n$. The matrix $\widetilde A-zI$ has block form
$$\begin{pmatrix}s_1^*s_1-z&s_1^*Y\\Y^*s_1&D\end{pmatrix}.$$
For a block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b^*\\b&D\end{pmatrix}$ with invertible $D$, solving its product with $(u,v)^T=(1,0)^T$ gives $v=-D^{-1}bu$ and $(a-b^*D^{-1}b)u=1$. Hence its inverse's upper-left entry is $(a-b^*D^{-1}b)^{-1}$. Here $(C_-)Y=YD$, so $(C_-)(I-YD^{-1}Y^*)=C_- -YY^*=-zI$ and $I-YD^{-1}Y^*=-zC_-^{-1}=-zR_1$. The Schur complement is therefore $s_1^*(I-YD^{-1}Y^*)s_1-z=-z(1+s_1^*R_1s_1)$, proving $(\widetilde R)_{11}=-\beta_1/z$.

By exchangeability of the columns and step 2.2, $zq=-N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbb E\beta_j$. The identity $R^{-1}=\sum_j s_js_j^*-zI$ gives $\sum_j s_js_j^*R=I+zR$. The rank-one formula [F2] gives $s_js_j^*R=\beta_js_js_j^*R_j$. Substituting these identities and the formula for $zq$ yields
$$\mathbb E R+\frac1zC=\frac1z\sum_{j=1}^N\mathbb E\left[\beta_j\left(Cs_js_j^*R_j-N^{-1}CT\,\mathbb E R\right)\right].$$
Testing against $x$ and adding then subtracting $N^{-1}x^*CTR_jx$ and $N^{-1}x^*CTRx$ decomposes the right side into three terms $\delta_1+\delta_2+\delta_3$.

For the first term, $\delta_1=(N/z)\mathbb E(\beta_1\alpha_1)$. Since $b_1$ is independent of column 1 and $\mathbb E_1\alpha_1=0$, we have $\mathbb E(b_1\alpha_1)=0$. Therefore step 2.1, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the uniform bounds on $\beta_1,b_1$ imply
$$|\delta_1|\le C_2N(\mathbb E|\xi_1|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E|\alpha_1|^2)^{1/2}=O(N^{-1/2}).$$

For the second term, $R_1-R=\beta_1R_1s_1s_1^*R_1$. Conditional second moments of the two linear forms $x^*CTR_1s_1$ and $s_1^*R_1x$ are each $O(N^{-1})$, uniformly in the other columns. Cauchy–Schwarz and boundedness of $\beta_1$ yield $|\delta_2|=O(N^{-1})$.

The third term is $\delta_3=z^{-1}\mathbb E[\beta_1x^*CT(R-\mathbb ER)x]$. Put $u=(CT)^*x$ and $v=x$; their norms are uniformly bounded by step 1.1. For $Q(w)=w^*(R-\mathbb ER)w$, direct expansion gives
$$u^*(R-\mathbb ER)v=\frac14\{Q(u+v)-Q(u-v)-iQ(u+iv)+iQ(u-iv)\}.$$
After rescaling these vectors, [F3] and the union bound give a tail bounded by $C_3/(t^4N^2)$ for this bilinear form; zero vectors contribute zero. It is also bounded deterministically by $2\|u\|\|v\|/\eta$. Integrating the tail after splitting at $t=N^{-1/2}$ gives $\mathbb E|u^*(R-\mathbb ER)v|^2=O(N^{-1})$. Since $\beta_1$ is bounded, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\delta_3|=O(N^{-1/2})$.
The bounds in steps 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3 tend to zero uniformly over deterministic unit $x$. The tested resolvent identity in step 3.1 therefore proves the asserted supremum limit.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For positive integers $n$ and $p$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and define its (uncentered, unit-variance-normalized) sample covariance matrix by
$$S(X):=\frac1nX^{\mathsf T}X\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}.$$
It is real symmetric and non-negative. If its eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are $\lambda_1(S(X)),\ldots,\lambda_p(S(X))$, its empirical spectral distribution (ESD), normalized by the matrix dimension $p$, is
$$\mu_{S(X)}:=\frac1p\sum_{j=1}^p\delta_{\lambda_j(S(X))}.$$
The largest eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\max}(S(X)):=\max_j\lambda_j(S(X))$. When $S(X)$ has at least one positive eigenvalue, its smallest positive eigenvalue is $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S(X)):=\min\{\lambda_j(S(X)):\lambda_j(S(X))>0\}$. For a sequence $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$, write $S_n=S(X_n)$ and $\mu_n=\mu_{S_n}$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. For $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, its Stieltjes transform, with the $(x-z)^{-1}$ convention, is
$$m_\mu(z):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x-z}\,d\mu(x).$$
The integral is finite because $|x-z|^{-1}\le\eta^{-1}$ for every real $x$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$, let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have entries from one common iid law with mean zero, second absolute moment one and $|X_{ij}|\le K$ almost surely for a fixed $K$, and let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite (self-adjoint with $v^*T_nv\ge0$ for every $v$) with induced Euclidean operator norm $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M$. Define
$$A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2},\qquad \widetilde A_n=N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n,$$
$$R_n(z)=(A_n-zI_n)^{-1},\qquad \widetilde R_n(z)=(\widetilde A_n-zI_{N_n})^{-1},\qquad q_n(z)=\mathbb E\left[N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\widetilde R_n(z)\right].$$
For every fixed $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, the matrix $I_n+q_n(z)T_n$ is invertible and
$$\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\left|x^*\left(\mathbb E R_n(z)+\frac1z(I_n+q_n(z)T_n)^{-1}\right)x\right|\longrightarrow0.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $Y_{n,1},\ldots,Y_{n,N_n}$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb C^n$, let $B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{N_n}Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^*$, and assume $N_n/n\to\kappa\in(0,\infty)$. Fix $z=u+i\eta$ with $u\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$, and define
$$M_n(z):=\frac1n\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}.$$
Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\}\le4\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2n^2\eta^2}{4N_n}\right),$$
and $M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)\to0$ almost surely.

Let $c>0$, let $H$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,\infty)$, and fix $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. There is at most one $q\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}q>0$, $u:=-(1-c)/z+cq$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$q=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czq)-z}\,dH(t).$$

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$, with Stieltjes transform $m_\mu(z)=\int (x-z)^{-1}\,d\mu(x)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. For every $a<b$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mu((a,b))+\tfrac12\mu(\{a\})+\tfrac12\mu(\{b\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du,\qquad \mu(\{x\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\eta\,\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta).$$
If two Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R$ have the same Stieltjes transform on the upper half-plane, then they are equal.

For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be a positive integer with $n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb C^{n\times N_n}$ have independent identically distributed entries $\xi$ satisfying $\mathbb E\xi=0$ and $|\xi|\le K$ almost surely for a fixed $K<\infty$. Then there is a finite constant $C=C(K,c)$ such that, almost surely, $\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\sqrt{N_n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For Hermitian $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, write their eigenvalues in
descending order with multiplicity as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(A)$
and $\lambda_1(B)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(B)$. Then, for every $j$,
$$|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|_2.$$

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: Write $c_n=n/N_n$, let $\bar F_n(B)=\mathbb E F_n(B)$, and let $\bar G_n$ be defined similarly for $\widetilde A_n=N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n$. By [F14], each ordered eigenvalue is continuous in the matrix entries, so these setwise expectations are defined for Borel $B$. For disjoint Borel sets, countable additivity of the random ESDs followed by [F13] gives countable additivity of $\bar F_n$ and $\bar G_n$; their total masses are one. Independence and unit second moment give $\int t\,d\bar F_n(t)=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}T_n$ and $\int t\,d\bar G_n(t)=N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}T_n$. Both first moments are uniformly bounded because $c_n\to c>0$ and $\|T_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is uniformly bounded. By [F4], their tails above $R$ are at most the corresponding first moment divided by $R$, so both expected-measure sequences are tight on $[0,\infty)$. The half-line is Polish: it is a closed subset of the complete real line and $\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)$ is dense. By [A1] and [F5], every subsequence of $\bar F_n$ has a further weakly convergent subsequence.

Fix $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and take any such subsequence with $\bar F_n\Rightarrow G$. Let $m_G(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}dG(t)$ and $q_n(z)=\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar G_n(t)$. By [F11], the two sample-covariance matrices have the same nonzero eigenvalues, so their transforms satisfy exactly $q_n=-(1-c_n)/z+c_n\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar F_n(t)$. Hence $q_n\to u:=-(1-c)/z+cm_G(z)$. Moreover $\operatorname{Im}m_G(z)>0$. The first moments of $\bar G_n$ are bounded, so at least half of each $\bar G_n$ lies in some fixed interval $[0,L]$; consequently $\operatorname{Im}q_n(z)\ge\eta/(2(L+|z|)^2)$ and $\operatorname{Im}u>0$.

Apply [F6] to an orthonormal eigenbasis of $T_n$. Its uniform quadratic-form error implies
$$\int(t-z)^{-1}\,d\bar F_n(t)=-\frac1{z n}\operatorname{tr}(I+q_nT_n)^{-1}+o(1)=-\frac1z\int\frac{1}{1+q_nt}\,dH_n(t)+o(1).$$
Since $H_n\Rightarrow H$, all $H_n$ are supported in one compact interval, $q_n\to u$, and $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, the integrands converge uniformly on that interval to $-1/[z(1+ut)]$. Thus $m_G(z)=\int[-z(1+ut)]^{-1}dH(t)$. The relation for $u$ in step 2.1 gives $-z(1+ut)=t(1-c-czm_G(z))-z$, so $m_G$ satisfies the fixed-point equation in the Statement. The argument applies to every $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and every weak subsequential limit $G$. By [F8], all such limits have the same transform; [F9] makes them equal. At least one such limit exists by step 1.1, so call it $F_{c,H}$. Tightness then implies $\bar F_n\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$.

For each fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$, [F7] gives $\int(t-z)^{-1}dF_n(t)-\int(t-z)^{-1}d\bar F_n(t)\to0$ almost surely. Intersect these probability-one events over the countable dense set $\{a+ib:a,b\in\mathbb Q,\ b>0\}$.

On the same event, [F10] gives $\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L_1$ eventually for a finite deterministic $L_1$, so the random measures $F_n$ are eventually supported on $[0,L_1]$ and are tight. The half-line is Polish by the metric facts in step 1.1 and [F15]. By [A1] and [F5], every subsequence has a weakly convergent further subsequence. For each dense-set $z$, its transform equals that of $F_{c,H}$ by steps 3.1 and 1.2, since the real and imaginary parts of $(t-z)^{-1}$ are bounded continuous and [F16] applies to each. For any probability law $\mu$, its transform satisfies $|m_\mu(z)-m_\mu(w)|\le |z-w|/(\operatorname{Im}z\operatorname{Im}w)$, so equality on the dense set extends to all $\mathbb C^+$; [F9] identifies the subsequential limit as $F_{c,H}$. Every subsequence has the same further limit, and [F16] gives $F_n\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$ almost surely.
